Issued at 303 AM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

THUNDERSTORM CHANCES: 

LATE THIS AFTERNOON-TONIGHT...A strong slow-moving cold front 
approaching from the north interacting with an unseasonably 
moist/unstable airmass will be the focus for scattered to numerous 
thunderstorms late this afternoon through tonight across portions of 
central, south-central, and southeast KS. Thinking the greatest 
hazard from this activity will be areas of heavy rainfall and 
localized flooding concerns, due to the very moist airmass and the 
potential for training showers/storms owing to the parallel 
orientation of the slow-moving front and mid-level flow. The latest 
CAMs suggest the most likely location for the highest rain totals 
will be roughly along and either side of Highway 50 south through 
about Highways 54/400 counties. Localized 3-5+ inch amounts seem 
possible, so we went ahead and hoisted a Flood Watch late this 
afternoon through about mid-morning Wednesday for the highest 
confidence counties.

Additionally in the same area as the heavy rainfall threat, a 
handful of strong to severe thunderstorms are expected late this 
afternoon through the evening, given the moderate to strong buoyancy 
and decent 40-50 kts of deep layer effective shear. Initial 
supercells have the potential to produce large hail and damaging 
winds. Can't completely rule out an isolated brief tornado, 
especially for any supercell structures that can maintain into the 
evening when the surface flow backs a bit and the low-level jet 
increases. After about 8-9 PM, thinking merging cold pools should 
transition the primary thunderstorm hazards to wind and marginal 
hail (along with continued heavy rainfall). Furthermore, will likely 
see additional shower/thunderstorm development well north of the 
surface front as the evening and night progress, with a continued 
threat for marginally severe hail given ample elevated instability 
and effective shear.

WEDNESDAY-THURSDAY MORNING...This period will feature off-and-on 
scattered to numerous showers/thunderstorms and areas of drizzle 
across the region, as a deep upper trough approaches slowly from the 
west, and the deep cold frontal zone stalls across the area. 
Continued unseasonably rich precipitable waters and strong forcing 
should lead to areas of heavy rainfall and possibly some localized 
flooding issues. Limited buoyancy should temper the overall severe 
weather potential. Did not have enough confidence to run the current 
Flood Watch out past early Wednesday, but later shifts may need to 
consider extending it through Thursday morning for portions of the 
area.

TEMPERATURES & WIND:

TODAY...This will be the last unseasonable warm day, with upper 80s 
to low 90s likely. May flirt with record highs at both Wichita and 
Chanute. In contrast, locations generally north of Great Bend to 
Salina will be much cooler in wake of the strong cold front, with 
60s and 70s likely. Had to significantly undercut NBM temperatures 
for today in these locations.

WEDNESDAY-THURSDAY...Had to undercut NBM high temperatures for 
Wednesday and Thursday as well, and probably not quite enough, due 
to widespread clouds/precipitation along with the strong potential 
for a further south placement of the cold front. Highs in the 60s-
70s are likely, warmest over southeast KS. However, central KS may 
not get out of the 50s. Stout/gusty north winds will expand 
southeast across the region Thursday in wake of this strong storm 
system.

FRIDAY-SATURDAY...A deepening central to eastern North American 
upper trough will drive strong Canadian high pressure south into Mid-
America, supporting the coolest air thus far this fall season. High 
temperatures in the 50s to lows 60s appear likely. Additionally, 
stout/gusty north winds Friday will make it feel even cooler. The 
coolest night will be Friday night, with lows likely dipping into 
the 30s to low 40s underneath the strong high pressure. Given the 
light winds and clear skies, added the potential for frost early 
Saturday generally along/north of Highway 50.

SUNDAY AND BEYOND...Model consensus supports a quick return to 
seasonable or even above normal temperatures, especially by next 
week, as another deep upper trough sets up over the western CONUS.
